documents.abstract: Three transformations are unfolding in India simultaneously, and this chapter argues that none of them can be fully understood, or wisely governed, in isolation from the other two. Artificial intelligence has moved, within a single decade, from a specialised research pursuit to a general-purpose technology reshaping how India teaches, works, and grows; the National Education Policy 2020 has committed the country to becoming a "knowledge society" through an ambitious, still-unfinished restructuring of school and higher education; and India's economic-policy establishment has begun treating AI-enabled growth and human-capital formation as a single connected project rather than two separate portfolios. This chapter synthesises evidence across all three domains - India's AI institutional architecture (the IndiaAI Mission, the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, and the 2026 India AI Impact Summit's New Delhi Declaration), NEP 2020's knowledge-economy targets (a fifty-per-cent higher-education Gross Enrolment Ratio by 2035, the National Credit Framework, and India's research-investment shortfall), and the international literature on AI, automation, and human capital formation - to assess how close India actually is to the "sustainable knowledge society" its own policy documents describe. It finds a pattern familiar from this volume's sector-specific chapters repeated here at macro scale: ambitious institutional design substantially outrunning measured, funded delivery, evident in an AI mission that has disbursed under four per cent of its five-year outlay and a research-and-development investment rate roughly a quarter of the level comparable innovation economies sustain. Rather than treating this gap as merely descriptive, the chapter closes with a dedicated set of policy recommendations addressed to the specific, evidenced shortfalls the preceding sections identify, arguing that closing the disbursement-and-delivery gap, not further expanding institutional ambition, is what now stands between India's stated knowledge-society vision and its realisation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered Chinese primary education faster than curricula, assessment systems and teacher preparation have adapted to it. While a growing body of Chinese scholarship explores how GenAI can “empower” yuwen (Chinese language) teaching, considerably less attention has been paid to the disruptive effects that frontline teachers must absorb in daily practice. This article offers a qualitative, interpretive analysis of how AI affects primary school Chinese language teaching when viewed from the teacher’s position. Rather than collecting new empirical data, it analyses three bodies of material: national and international policy documents on GenAI in schools, Chinese and international research on AI in language and primary education, and published expert commentary on Chinese language education in the AI era. Read through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the analysis identifies four interrelated areas of impact: the erosion of foundational literacy practices such as character writing and sustained reading; a crisis of authorship in writing instruction, in which teachers are pushed from cultivating expression towards verifying authenticity; the reconfiguration of teachers’ professional roles and identities; and institutional ambiguity arising from gaps between national policy, school practice, assessment and home use. The article argues that the central difficulty is not technological access but a misalignment between AI-saturated learning environments and product-oriented teaching and assessment traditions. Implications are drawn for process-oriented writing pedagogy, assessment reform, teacher professional development and home–school collaboration.

AbstractGenerative AI can now create maps, explain geographical concepts, generate spatial visualizations, assist GIS workflows, write code, interpret satellite imagery and transform natural-language instructions into geospatial outputs. This capability creates a fundamental educational question: if AI can increasingly perform tasks traditionally taught to geography students, what geographical skills should students learn in the future? This paper critically investigates this question through a systematic synthesis of emerging empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks and future scenarios. Drawing on studies of AI-assisted spatial thinking, GIS education, cartographic literacy and cognitive offloading, the paper argues that Generative AI may shift geography education from teaching students primarily how to produce maps toward teaching students how to critically conceptualize, validate, interrogate and ethically use AI-generated geospatial representations. The paper proposes an original conceptual framework—the Generative AI–Geography Education Transformation Model (GAIGETM)—and develops evidence-based 2030–2050 scenarios. It concludes that the future of geography education depends not on whether AI can make maps, but on whether educational systems can teach students to question, validate, interpret and critically reason about the maps that AI produces.

Introduction. The adoption of generative AI raises ethical concerns for information professionals whose intermediary role requires them to ensure information quality standards that users cannot independently verify. Professional ethics address quality superficially, and the ethical implications of generative AI have not been examined from the perspective of professional obligations. Method. A scoping review assessed 644 records across three search strands, retaining 120 papers, which were analysed against ten information quality criteria and assessed for the strength of their ethical framing. Analysis. Ten practice-derived quality criteria, corresponding closely to ISO/IEC 25012, are shown to be based on a Kantian deontological framework complemented by a Marxist treatment of algorithmic surplus value. For each criterion the literature documenting the relevant AI failure mode is reviewed and its ethical treatment assessed. Results. Four criteria, accuracy, objectivity, identifiable origin, and accessibility, attract substantial ethical attention. For the remaining six, ethical treatment is limited or absent. Conclusions. The information professional's intermediary role is an ethical necessity. Professional organisations are called upon to lobby actively for AI governance using the criteria framework developed here.

documents.abstract: This scientific thesis examines the transformative impact of digital pedagogy and artificial intelligence (AI) integration within modern higher education systems. As educational paradigms shift from traditional instructor-centric models toward personalized, technology-enhanced learning environments, understanding the pedagogical, methodological, and psychological implications becomes critical. The study evaluates adaptive learning platforms, digital assessment tools, and AI-driven instructional scaffolding across diverse academic contexts. Employing a mixed-methods approach comprising empirical classroom surveys, literature synthesis, and qualitative faculty interviews, the research highlights key drivers of student engagement, academic performance retention, and critical thinking development. The findings demonstrate a 28% increase in conceptual retention when digital interactive tools are combined with active learning frameworks. However, significant challenges persist, including digital inequality, algorithmic bias, and the potential degradation of human-to-human pedagogical rapport. The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for curriculum designers, institutional policymakers, and educators aiming to establish an ethically sound, technologically robust educational ecosystem.

This community service program aims to empower batik artisans, particularly female MSMEs in Kemijen and Kampoeng Batik Semarang, by educating them on utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an assistive technology to design Semarangan batik motifs based on local wisdom. An interdisciplinary team spanning Communication Science, Cultural Studies, English, and Visual Communication Design implemented this program. The execution methods included conceptual counseling, practical training on generative AI, project-based creative mentoring, and design evaluations. The results demonstrated a significant increase in digital literacy: 100% of participants understood AI's role as an assistive design tool, and practical AI operational skills rose to 86%. The program successfully produced more than 5 collaborative batik motif prototypes (e.g., Warak Ngendog, blekok, and tamarind tree) and digital promotion copywriting in English. Program outputs include an ISBN-registered interdisciplinary educational module, an Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) registration draft for the educational model, and a scientific article draft submitted to a national Sinta 5 accredited journal. In conclusion, utilizing AI as an assistive technology accelerates visual design exploration without diluting local cultural philosophy and authenticity, thereby strengthening the economic resilience and digital capacity of female batik MSMEs in the creative industry. Keywords--- Artificial Intelligence (AI), Semarangan Batik, female MSMEs, local wisdom, community empowerment.

The paper addresses the ethical integration of artificial intelligence into philosophical counseling in Romania. We begin with the criteria used by Julia Clare and Richard Sivil to distinguish between practice and profession, and with the roadmap for recognizing the new profession of philosophical counseling in Romania, outlined in 2019 by Vasile Hațegan. Much of this process has already been accomplished; what remains is the cognitive dimension, which has yet to catch up with either online or algorithmically assisted practice. In the second part of the article, we draw upon Hațegan’s comparisons between philosophical counseling and psychotherapy, coaching, spiritual counseling, and mediation to identify five distinguishing criteria: counselor neutrality, the relational nature of the process, non-dependency, the non-therapeutic nature of the practice, and client autonomy. We treat these criteria as an ethical test for conversational AI agents. The APPAgpt platform proves particularly useful in this endeavor; through it, the American Philosophical Practitioners Association invites the public to converse with bots simulating dialogues with great thinkers, while simultaneously emphasizing the importance of the human counselor. The test yields nuanced results. When used by the counselor as a tool, artificial intelligence can operate within the boundaries of the practice; however, when placed in the counselor's role facing the client, it exceeds those limits. The article concludes with proposals for future occupational standards and the philosophical counselor's code of ethics: the inclusion of a competency unit dedicated to digitally mediated practice, as well as a decision-making procedure inspired by Henk van Luijk’s model.

documents.abstract: Leadership coaching develops managers but is expensive and difficult to scale. AI may be able to help scale access, but “answering machine” like AI coaching agents invite cognitive offloading and weaken learning. We instantiated a human coaching protocol, supported across prior cycles, as a text-based AI coach built to prompt reflective questioning. In the fourth cycle of a design-based research program at a global consulting firm, eight managers received the same protocol from a human coach and the AI coach, applied each session in an observed onboarding activity, and reflected on both in interviews. All eight welcomed the probing questions and preferred the human coach. Notably, they resisted the same protocol of questioning from the AI coach and wanted answers from it instead. This study’s theoretical contribution is the Reflection Penalty, the cost an AI coach pays for asking a user to do the reflective work that makes human coaching effective. Its practical contribution is a jobs-to-be-done map for AI coaching, assembled from proposals participants raised on their own. It divides coaching into distinct jobs and assigns each to the human or the AI best suited to it. Both contributions are offered to those designing AI tools that aim to support reflection

This study examined the relationship between intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation and academic achievement among NCE students of FCT College of Education, Abuja. A correlational survey research design was adopted, as the study sought to determine the extent and direction of the relationship among intrinsic, extrinsic motivation and students’ academic achievement. The population comprised 1,704 NCE II students, from which a sample of 313 students was drawn using the Krejcie and Morgan (1970) table and stratified and simple random sampling techniques was used in selecting the respondents fairly. A total of 311 questionnaires, representing 99.5% of the sampled respondents, were correctly completed and returned. Data were collected using a researcher-developed 30-item structured questionnaire divided into three sections: students’ cumulative grade point average (CGPA), 15 items measuring intrinsic motivation, and 15 items measuring extrinsic motivation. The instrument was face and content validated by experts, yielding a validity index of 0.76, and its reliability was established through a pilot study using Cronbach’s Alpha, which yielded coefficients of 0.93 and 0.88 for intrinsic and extrinsic motivation respectively. Data were analysed using Pearson Product Moment Correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed a weak to moderate, positive and significant relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation (r = .385, p < .05); a strong, positive and significant relationship between intrinsic motivation and academic achievement (r = .764, p < .05); and a strong, positive and significant relationship between extrinsic motivation and academic achievement (r = .629, p < .05). Consequently, the three null hypotheses were rejected. The study concluded that both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation are significantly associated with academic achievement. It was recommended that lecturers and school authorities design tasks that are interesting and engaging, employ inquiry-based and student-centred teaching methods, and clearly communicate the career benefits of academic success to enhance student motivation and performance.

Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used to interpret professional situations, formulate arguments, and consider responses to ethical dilemmas. Although these systems can broaden reflection, their persuasive outputs may encourage moral outsourcing, defined as transferring substantive elements of ethical interpretation, justification, or judgment to an external system without adequate examination, endorsement, or responsibility. This conceptual article asks how generative AI can be integrated into philosophical counseling and ethical reflection in teacher education without undermining ethical self-authorship. Drawing on philosophical counseling, moral development, relational autonomy, professional ethics, and AI literacy, it develops the Ethical Self-Authorship Cycle. The model comprises five iterative stages: articulating the dilemma, pluralizing perspectives, interrogating assumptions, testing reasons and consequences, and reclaiming moral authorship. Its contribution is threefold. First, it distributes deliberative functions between the human participant and AI by specifying what the system may contribute and what it cannot establish at each stage. Second, it requires the process to conclude with a human-formulated justification rather than an AI-generated recommendation. Third, it treats ethical self-authorship as a developing capacity requiring pedagogical scaffolding and ethically and digitally prepared teacher educators. An illustrative case demonstrates the model’s application to a dilemma involving student use of AI in assessment. The article argues that AI may generate material for ethical inquiry, but it cannot represent affected people, determine which values should prevail, or assume professional responsibility. Moral authorship and answerability must remain human.

documents.abstract: Abstract This article synthesizes proceedings and outcomes from the 2nd Pracademic Emergency Management and Homeland Security Summit, hosted virtually by Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University’s Worldwide Campus College of Arts & Sciences and its Virtual Collaboratory for Security and Resilience Education, Research, and Engagement. Drawing on contributions from an international and interdisciplinary group of scholars, practitioners, students, policymakers, and professional organizations representing higher education, government, industry, and operational practice, the summit examined emerging challenges and future directions across homeland security, emergency management, resilience, public health, homeland defense, disaster planning, information disorder, artificial intelligence, ethics, and standards development. Several cross-cutting findings emerged. First, preparedness and resilience increasingly require adaptive, inclusive, and whole-community approaches grounded in trusted communication, social capital, functional needs inclusion, and meaningful stakeholder engagement. Second, while artificial intelligence, remote sensing, and advanced decision-support systems offer substantial operational promise, their implementation demands stronger attention to ethical oversight, interoperability, governance, and consensus-based standards capable of translating technical capability into operational relevance. Third, increasingly complex threat environments reinforce the need for critical thinking, scenario-based learning, ethical reasoning, and career-long professional development to prepare leaders to operate across institutional boundaries and under incomplete information.

Background The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has created an ontological disruption in higher education, challenging traditional pedagogical mediation and academic production. This study examines the transformation of the teaching role in university environments across Peru, Chile, and Colombia, addressing a knowledge gap in Latin American empirical research regarding faculty perceptions and daily practices with Large Language Models. Methods The research employed a descriptive-interpretative qualitative design with an open-ended survey approach interpreted through a hermeneutic lens. A non-probabilistic sample of 48 undergraduate and graduate professors from 20 Higher Education Institutions in the region participated. Data were collected through a validated 18-item structured online questionnaire and analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis assisted by Atlas.ti software. Results The findings identify a transition from traditional instructional roles toward a “mediator-curator” model, where educators act as orchestrators of human-AI co-intelligence. Key applications include pedagogical re-engineering, such as dynamic curricular design, Socratic tutoring, and the shift from product-oriented to process-oriented assessment. Critical dimensions emerged regarding the need for pedagogical re-engineering, ethical challenges in academic integrity, and the development of critical AI literacy. National variations showed Chile focusing on pedagogical equity, Colombia on research productivity, and Peru on didactic agility. Conclusions The integration of GenAI in the Latin American university context requires a situated pedagogical response that transcends instrumental use. The study proposes a new learning ecology where the teacher facilitates critical interaction between students and generative systems. This shift necessitates a reconfiguration of teaching competencies toward epistemic curation and algorithmic responsibility to ensure meaningful and ethical learning.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a major technological force in the modern knowledge system. AI is transforming the way knowledge is discovered, organized, analyzed, disseminated, and preserved. Academic libraries in higher education are also an important part of this transformation. Technologies such as generative AI, intelligent information retrieval systems, AI-based chatbots, automated metadata generation, and digital repositories can make library services more efficient and user-centric. However, the use of AI has also created challenges such as information accuracy, data privacy, copyright, intellectual property, plagiarism, algorithmic bias, and digital inequality. Therefore, it is necessary to use AI in an ethical, safe, transparent, and human-centered manner, not just as a technological advancement. UNESCO (2023) has emphasized the importance of a human-centered approach, data privacy, and inclusion in the use of generative AI in education and research. This article has done a conceptual study of AI, higher education, National Education Policy 2020, open knowledge, information ethics, research integrity and inclusive library services. Based on this study, the concept of 'Human-Centric AI Library Ecosystem' has been proposed. Its main pillars are intelligent information search, open knowledge infrastructure, research integrity, ethical data management, inclusive access and continuous skill development of librarians.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and augmented reality (AR) in educational technology has opened new opportunities for enhancing constructivist learning, particularly in computer network education. This study aimed to design, develop, and evaluate Comnet-Art, an AI-based AR learning application, to improve students' understanding and constructivist skills in computer networks. The research involved 234 undergraduate students and employed the ADDIE model (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) along with expert validation, practicality testing, and effectiveness assessment. Validation results indicated strong content and media validity, with average Aiken's V scores of 0.92 from media experts and 0.89 from material experts, categorized as very valid. Practicality assessments revealed high usability and engagement, with educators reporting an average practicality score of 91.85% and students 90.71%. Effectiveness evaluation using pre-test and post-test comparisons demonstrated substantial learning gains, with the mean score increasing from 68.21 to 86.47 and a relative improvement of 26.76%, confirming the application's effectiveness in fostering engagement, collaboration, problem-solving, and constructivist learning outcomes. These findings highlight that Comnet-Art successfully integrates AI-driven interactivity and AR visualization to support active learning, improve conceptual understanding, and enhance higher-order cognitive skills. This study provides strong evidence that emerging technologies such as AI and AR can be effectively leveraged to transform engineering education and promote constructivist learning.

Context: Generative-AI coding assistants have moved rapidly into software development practice, raising human-factor questions about trust, usability, and responsible adoption that lab studies and surveys do not fully answer; sustained turn-by-turn production traces remain rare. Objective: This study examines four human-factor dimensions of sustained generative-AI-assisted development — trust calibration, developer gating, delegation-related prompt dynamics, and authorial identity — in a real production setting. Methods: Longitudinal autoethnography of a 16-month single-developer construction of a cloud-native institutional service at a Taiwanese university (424 git commits, Dec 2024 – Apr 2026), with two prompt corpora across two IDE-mediated assistants used in succession: 172 user prompts plus 2777 assistant turns from Cursor IDE (Sep–Dec 2025), and 50 user prompts from Claude Code CLI (Apr 2026). Per-session formal indicators (Eqs. (1) , (2) , (3) , (4) , (5) ), an analysis of a pre-stated directional prediction (Section 5.3 ), and triangulation with a companion architectural analysis (Chi, 2026) constrain interpretation. Results: (T) Trust calibration — in the trace-documented stuck-loop episode, the developer escalated model tier rather than revising specification (a capacity-oriented escalation). (G) Gating — the agent iteration ratio rises with task ambiguity, consistent with reduced developer gating of the agent loop when prompting is under-specified. (D) Delegation — within the Cursor window, prompt length compresses by up to 98.7% within a session (first to last third) while rewrite signals do not consistently decline, and prompt-skill improvement is not measurable under the study’s indicators, a pattern interpreted as consistent with a shift from prompting toward delegation rather than a direct measurement of it; in the later Claude Code window, 33 of 50 prompts are follow-ups (66%), a cross-tool observation reported descriptively. (I) Identity diffusion — authoring voice in commit messages converges toward the assistant’s register. Conclusion: Engineering throughput appeared to decouple from the developer-side communication indicators across the period; potential developer-side effects of sustained AI assistance may not register in conventional engineering metrics, supporting a cautionary reading for human-factor-aware adoption. All quantitative magnitudes reported are observations from one case; the four dimensions are offered for analytical generalization, as hypotheses for multi-developer studies to test, not as evidence of general developer behaviour. The article closes with responsible-adoption implications for IDE-assistant design.

The exponential growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cloud computing technologies has revolutionized data processing and intelligent service delivery at scale. Organizations across virtually every sector now rely on cloud-hosted machine learning pipelines to extract value from data that is collected continuously, at volumes and velocities that on-premises infrastructure struggles to match. However, this technological advancement comes with significant challenges, particularly concerning privacy and security of sensitive data transmitted to cloud environments. This research paper addresses the critical intersection of trustworthy cloud infrastructure and privacy-preserving artificial intelligence processing. Our work explores a comprehensive framework that integrates privacy protection mechanisms, secure computation techniques, and confidence assessment measures to establish reliable and trustworthy AI services in cloud environments. We propose that by combining differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, and confidence-aware prediction mechanisms, organizations can maintain data confidentiality while leveraging the computational power of cloud-based AI systems. Rather than treating privacy, security, and reliability as separate concerns to be bolted onto a finished system, the framework proposed here treats them as first-class design requirements that shape every layer of the processing pipeline, from data ingestion through model inference to the communication of results back to end users. This study examines existing privacy-preserving techniques applicable to cloud AI, analyzes their performance trade-offs, and evaluates the reliability of AI predictions through confidence scoring. Our findings demonstrate that it is possible to achieve a balanced approach where sensitive data remains protected, AI model performance remains acceptable, and computational overhead is manageable. The research contributes to the development of secure, trustworthy AI solutions suitable for healthcare, financial services, educational institutions, and other sectors requiring stringent privacy compliance. We further situate our contribution within the broader movement toward trustworthy and responsible AI, arguing that privacy-preservation is not merely a compliance checkbox but a foundational property that determines whether AI systems can be adopted at scale in sensitive domains.

documents.abstract: AI can improve the quality and speed of work without establishing whether people are developing the judgement needed to examine evidence, recognise omissions and respond appropriately when circumstances change. This whitepaper examines how AI can remove, enrich or relocate the experiences through which judgement develops. Drawing on research into workplace learning, expertise, AI-assisted performance and human oversight, it distinguishes assisted output from retained understanding and transferable judgement. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can accelerate knowledge-work tasks, but task-level efficiency does not necessarily translate into shorter working hours or improved employee welfare. This article proposes an AI time-dividend allocation framework that separates the creation of saved time from its subsequent use. Drawing on the job demands–resources perspective, it examines a resource pathway through perceived time savings and work–life balance alongside a competing demand pathway through work intensification. The reported three-wave observational survey comprises 472 complete cases. Standardized ordinary least squares models with HC3 robust standard errors indicate that GenAI use intensity is associated with perceived time savings (β = .495, p < .001). Time savings is positively associated with work–life balance (β = .255, p < .001), whereas work intensification is negatively associated with work–life balance (β = −.443, p < .001). Reported bootstrap indirect effects are positive through time savings (0.126, 95% CI [0.079, 0.176]) and negative through time savings and work intensification (−0.036, 95% CI [−0.059, −0.015]). Performance pressure is positively associated with intensification, but its proposed interaction with time savings is not statistically significant. The findings are consistent with competing allocation pathways; given the observational design, they should not be interpreted as causal effects. The article identifies time-dividend allocation as a consequential dimension of AI-enabled work design.

This study examines the effects of work environment, work supervision, and job training on occupational safety and health (K3) and work productivity, as well as the effect of K3 on work productivity among 200 employees at CV Griya Fajar Konstruksi, South Tangerang. A quantitative approach was employed using survey data from 200 employees and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The results show that work environment and work supervision have positive and statistically significant effects on K3 and work productivity, while K3 has the strongest positive relationship with work productivity (β = 0.989; p < 0.001). In contrast, job training shows negative and statistically significant relationships with K3 (β = −0.437; p = 0.034) and work productivity (β = −0.285; p = 0.041). Five of the seven hypotheses are supported. The findings qualify the expected positive role of training by indicating that its provision alone does not necessarily translate into improved safety and productivity. The findings also highlight the importance of integrating supportive working conditions, consistent supervision, effective K3 practices, and relevant and practical training to support safe and productive construction operations.

documents.abstract: This study compared the image-based workplace safety judgments of three general-purpose AI assistants across five occupational contexts. Fifteen workplace images representing construction, workshop/manufacturing, maintenance/technical service, warehouse/logistics, and laboratory settings were evaluated by ChatGPT GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.5 Flash. Each model completed 15 single-image assessments and five within-context relative-ranking tasks, yielding 60 outputs. Two occupational safety specialists independently rated the outputs on five 0–5 dimensions and six binary error patterns. The raters showed exact or near-exact score agreement in 81.8% of the ordinal ratings; pooled quadratic weighted agreement was moderate, κ = 0.479, 95% CI [0.340, 0.595]. Agreement was complete for pairwise ranking accuracy and exact final ordering. Based on the two-rater means, ChatGPT led in visible evidence coverage (4.37), visual fidelity (4.43), prioritization (3.73), and uncertainty discipline (4.70), whereas Claude obtained the highest descriptive control-guidance mean (4.40). Between-model differences were statistically significant in the other four dimensions but not in control guidance. No rater-confirmed problematic control recommendation was observed. All three models achieved the same final-match performance: four of five context rankings were fully correct and 14 of 15 pairwise relations were correct. The shared failure occurred in the workshop/manufacturing context, where the image containing a visible person at height was ranked below a dusty but static scene. The findings support supervised first-pass use of AI assistants but not autonomous workplace safety evaluation.

ABSTRACT Background Writing motivation and self‐efficacy are critical factors of success in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts, yet they are frequently undermined by learner anxiety and limited teacher feedback. While artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots offer potential for adaptive writing support, limited research has examined these affective constructs in parallel across learner proficiency levels. Objectives This study investigated changes in intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy among high school EFL learners at higher‐ and lower‐proficiency levels following chatbot‐supported writing and examined whether these changes differed across proficiency levels. Methods Using an exploratory mixed‐methods design, the study involved 47 Vietnamese high school students divided into higher‐ and lower‐proficiency level groups. Over the 11‐week study, participants completed 8 weeks of AI‐supported writing activities using a chatbot designed in accordance with principles of Self‐Determination Theory, Self‐Regulated Learning Theory and Self‐Efficacy Theory. Changes in intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy were examined using pre‐ and post‐questionnaires and semi‐structured interviews. Results and Conclusions The quantitative findings revealed that intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy increased over time in both proficiency groups, with no significant differences in the magnitude of change between higher‐ and lower‐proficiency learners. This suggests that the affective changes observed during AI‐supported writing were not confined to one proficiency group. The qualitative findings indicated that learners linked their positive experiences to reduced anxiety, clearer guidance, and supportive interaction, although the types of support they valued differed by proficiency level. Overall, the findings suggest that when positioned as a supportive writing partner rather than an answer generator, AI chatbot feedback may be associated with positive motivational and self‐efficacy development in mixed‐ability EFL writing classrooms.

Ergonomics in the field of occupational safety is a scientific discipline that focuses on ensuring comfortable and safe working conditions. It studies the interaction between people, technology, and the environment, aiming to adapt workplaces to employees’ physical and cognitive capabilities. The primary goal of ergonomics is to protect workers’ health, reduce fatigue, and improve the safety and efficiency of the work process. Research in this field is aimed at creating safe, comfortable, and highly efficient working conditions. This helps preserve workers’ health and increase their productivity. Ergonomics views people, technology, and the environment as a single system; analyzes the work process through the sequence of an operator’s actions, goals, and tasks; adapts equipment and furniture to human anatomy; and studies fatigue and the strain on the nervous system and the senses. This scientific article analyzes occupational ergonomics as an interdisciplinary science that studies human interaction with the work environment to improve efficiency, safety, and comfort. The term “ergonomics” was coined by Wojciech Jastrzębski in the 19th century, while in the 20th century, this discipline evolved into an independent science due to industrial and military demands following World War II. Current trends include adapting to digitalization, automation, and remote work, highlighting the importance of cognitive ergonomics and human-machine interaction. The economic aspect underscores the cost-effectiveness of ergonomic solutions: reducing injuries and absenteeism, as well as increasing productivity, leads to savings in labor costs. The article offers practical recommendations, such as personalizing workstations and applying modern technologies, and identifies areas for further research on integrating ergonomic principles into cutting-edge technologies, particularly virtual reality and artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: This article examines socio-psychological factors associated with school students’ cognitive activity. It discusses family support, teacher–student interaction, peer relationships, learning motivation, and classroom psychological climate. The aim is to identify and systematize the main factors through theoretical analysis. The study uses comparison and synthesis of scientific literature. Drawing on Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, Bandura’s social cognitive theory, and Deci and Ryan’s self-determination theory, the article outlines conditions that may support students’ cognitive engagement. No experimental data are reported. The theoretical conclusions may inform psychological and pedagogical practices in schools.

Web-based technologies often fail to fundamentally reshape teaching processes, despite their ubiquity. This study presents a dual-loop intelligent teaching assistant system that integrates natural language processing-driven intent recognition and sentiment analysis within a human-in-the-loop framework. Unlike systems prioritizing pure automation, this study's architecture dynamically routes complex queries to instructors via a visual decision-support dashboard, balancing real-time responsiveness with pedagogical nuance. Empirical results in higher education reveal that while interaction efficiency improved significantly, user satisfaction depended nonlinearly on technical accuracy, heavily influenced by notification strategies and emergent student behaviors, like reverse engineering the bot. These findings underscore the need to evolve web-based tools from static utilities into adaptive sociotechnical ecosystems that actively support both learner autonomy and instructor decision-making.

documents.abstract: Background The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in U.S. hospitals has outpaced regulatory frameworks. By end-2025, the FDA had authorized over 1,451 AI-enabled medical devices, yet governance remains fragmented and reactive. Although the regulatory analysis focuses on the United States, the review included international evidence where directly relevant to U.S. hospital governance, and U.S.-specific conclusions rest primarily on the U.S.-based evidence. Objectives This systematic review and regulatory gap analysis examined the current state of AI governance in U.S. hospitals, identified critical gaps between existing regulations and governance needs, and proposed a comprehensive framework for safe and trustworthy AI deployment. Methods The review was conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar) were searched for peer-reviewed articles published from January 2017 through January 2026 (final searches 15–18 January 2026). The PICOS framework structured inclusion criteria. Quality was assessed using CASP, NOS, and QUADAS-2 according to study design. A narrative synthesis approach was employed, followed by a structured regulatory gap analysis of federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. Results Of 1,065 records identified, 22 studies met the eligibility criteria. In the systematic review, FDA, ONC, and CMS standards were inconsistent and poorly tailored to AI's evolving capabilities, with evidence of inconsistency between pre-market approval and real-world performance, underutilization of continuous surveillance, and failure to conduct subgroup bias analyses. The regulatory gap analysis identified four critical gaps: post-market surveillance deficiencies, equity protection failures, accountability clarification shortcomings, and governance capacity disparities. Interpretation of these findings for U.S. regulatory policy is provided separately in the regulatory gap analysis and the Discussion. Conclusion A lifecycle governance framework is needed, incorporating continuous monitoring, transparency assurance, equity safeguards, accountability mechanisms, and scalable governance structures to ensure safe, ethical, and trustworthy AI deployment in healthcare. Key limitations include the retrospective protocol registration, the restriction to English-language publications, and the heterogeneity of the included evidence. documents.abstract: This statement from Harmondeg Philosophy responds to the October 13, 2026 open letter signed by 406 scientists calling for stronger safeguards for advanced artificial intelligence, including the isolation of certain high-risk AI systems from the internet. The statement recognizes the importance of scientific concern, responsible risk assessment, and effective containment measures. It argues, however, that lasting AI safety requires a more fundamental reconsideration of the philosophical foundations through which artificial intelligence is understood, investigated, and governed. Drawing on the principle of Civilizational Responsibility Consciousness, previously advanced in Saving the Soul of Science: From Unleashing Power to Safeguarding Civilization, the statement calls for scientific creation to be evaluated in light of both its constructive potential and its possible consequences for present and future generations. It advances four fundamental judgments from Harmondeg Philosophy: Artificial intelligence represents the material realization, extension, and amplification of human intellectual capacities, with the potential to extend human physical capabilities. The fundamental purpose of AI development is the well-being of all humanity, including those whose employment, livelihoods, and conditions of existence are transformed by technological change. AI must become a core scientific and technological force safeguarding the safety, stability, and enduring development of human civilization. AI is an indispensable pathway toward humanity's transition into the space age and the age of deep-space civilization. The statement maintains that AI can be understood and governed through deeper philosophical inquiry, scientific investigation, and the development of effective safety and governance capabilities. It invites international discussion, independent evaluation, and cooperation while affirming the need for both safer and more powerful AI. The publication includes English and Chinese versions. documents.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has created new opportunities for improving teacher preparation and developing professional competence among future English language teachers. AI-enhanced learning environments provide innovative tools for personalized instruction, adaptive learning, automated feedback, language assessment, and the development of digital pedagogical skills. However, the effective use of these technologies requires a systematic methodological framework that combines linguistic knowledge, pedagogical expertise, digital literacy, and ethical awareness. This thesis aims to examine the key methodological principles and structural components of a framework for developing the professional competence of future English language teachers in AI-enhanced learning environments. Particular attention is given to the integration of AI-based educational tools, learner-centered approaches, reflective practice, and competency-based instruction. The proposed framework emphasizes the importance of preparing prospective teachers to use AI critically, responsibly, and effectively in English language teaching. The study concludes that the purposeful integration of AI technologies into teacher education can support the development of professional autonomy, instructional creativity, and readiness for digital transformation in education.

This deposit presents a proposed practice methodology for structured human–AI inquiry, developed from Kon Lionis’s A Participatory Framework for Human-AI Co-Inquiry. The methodology organises an inquiry episode around five stages: orient and frame; explore and distinguish; apply productive friction; ground and diagnose; and audit, revise, and close. It combines exploratory dialogue with explicit assumptions, substantive challenge, appropriate checking, and traceable revision. A central distinction is between a claim’s category and its verification status: identifying something as a factual claim does not establish that it is true. The procedure also separates completing the required steps from answering the question. Agreement, fluent explanation, and complete documentation do not by themselves establish evidential support. Two complementary documents are included: • Full methodology — working draft v0.2, dated 13 October 2026. Sets out the stages, participant responsibilities, claim ledger, verification priorities, closing decisions, documentation requirements, and proposed evaluation approach. It includes guidance for assessing understanding and developing bounded research leads. • Lite companion — working draft v0.3, dated 14 October 2026. Provides a self-contained prompt block for interactive use in an AI conversation, with Quick and Standard depths and referral to the full methodology for consequential inquiries. It retains the central safeguards while reducing record-keeping. Both versions require assumptions and hypothetical premises to retain their status throughout the conversation. When evidence, tools, time, or expertise are insufficient, conclusions must be narrowed, made conditional, or suspended. Available closing outcomes are Close, Iterate, Escalate, and Abstain. These documents are working drafts offered for practical use, criticism, adaptation, and empirical evaluation. They do not report a completed validation study or establish improvements in accuracy, understanding, or efficiency. They make no claim that AI systems possess subjective awareness or that a model’s limitations define the limits of human knowledge. Question everything, including the question.

documents.abstract: The transition from preclinical to clinical training is a critical and challenging phase in medical education, during which students encounter new clinical, professional, and organizational demands. Transition to Clerkship Courses (TCC) have been developed to support students during this transition, but relatively few have explicitly incorporated a motivational framework into curriculum development. This study describes the development and implementation of a Self-Determination Theory (SDT) informed TCC and reports students’ descriptive post-course motivational characteristics. This curriculum design and implementation study was conducted at Al-Subtain University of Medical Sciences, Karbala, Iraq, involving 108 medical students transitioning to clerkship. The TCC was developed using Kern’s six-step model: (1) problem identification and general needs assessment through literature review; (2) targeted needs assessment via focus groups; (3) formulation of goals and objectives; (4) development of SDT-informed educational strategies; (5) implementation through a structured three-module course; and (6) evaluation. The curriculum was explicitly aligned with SDT’s psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) and delivered using autonomy-supportive teaching strategies. The curriculum incorporated autonomy-supportive practices (e.g., offering meaningful choices and rationales), competence-supportive strategies (e.g., scaffolded skill practice and formative feedback), and relatedness-supportive approaches (e.g., small-group learning and near-peer mentoring) to create a need-supportive learning environment. Evaluation was conducted descriptively using the Academic Motivation Scale. The literature review identified recurring educational needs related to clinical logistics, procedural preparation, and formative learning support. The targeted needs assessment informed curriculum priorities that were subsequently mapped onto SDT’s concepts of autonomy, competence, and relatedness. A three-module TCC addressing hospital orientation, procedural skills, and professionalism and communication was implemented for 108 students. The post-course AMS results showed relatively higher scores across intrinsic motivation and identified regulation alongside relatively high controlled forms of motivation, with amotivation showing the lowest mean score. This study illustrates how Kern’s six-step curriculum-development framework can be combined with SDT principles to inform the design and implementation of a transition to clerkship curriculum. The approach provides an example of how motivational theory can be incorporated into curriculum development for the transition to clinical training.

Introduction Although collaborative robots can safely share workspaces with human operators, most collaborative workstations remain static and cannot adapt to changes in operator posture during task execution, potentially compromising ergonomics and interaction quality. This study presents a vision-guided closed-loop adaptive control framework that enables a collaborative robot to continuously adjust workpiece position according to the operator’s posture. Methods Using real-time vision-based human pose estimation, the system automatically modifies workpiece height and reach distance to support ergonomic working postures. The framework was evaluated with 30 participants performing screw-driving tasks under fixed and adaptive workstation conditions. Results Compared with the fixed workstation, the adaptive workstation significantly reduced Rapid Upper Limb Assessment scores, improved physical comfort, reduced perceived postural load, and increased trust and acceptance without compromising perceived safety. In addition, it reduced the influence of participant height on ergonomic performance, demonstrating improved anthropometric adaptability. Discussion These findings demonstrate that real-time posture perception can serve as an effective feedback mechanism for adaptive robot control, providing a practical framework for human-centered collaborative workstations that accommodate operator variability while improving ergonomic outcomes and user experience.

Objective With the widespread application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, academic emotions play a vital role in students’ learning processes. This study aims to examine the associations between positive and negative academic emotions and college students’ perceived learning outcomes, and analyze the serial mediating roles of AI acceptance and learning behaviors within GenAI-supported learning environments. Methods A total of 526 college students with GenAI learning experience were recruited via convenience sampling. All participants completed four standardized scales measuring academic emotions, AI acceptance, learning behaviors and perceived learning outcomes. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, confirmatory factor analysis and bias-corrected Bootstrap mediation tests were conducted using SPSS 26.0 and AMOS 27.0. Results All variables were significantly correlated ( p < 0.01). Positive academic emotions exerted a significant direct association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.176), whereas the direct association of negative academic emotions was non-significant ( β = −0.098, p = 0.049, 95% CI [−0.205, 0.007]). AI acceptance and learning behaviors had significant independent mediating effects. The serial mediation effect value was 0.020 for positive emotions and −0.037 for negative emotions, with all 95% confidence intervals excluding zero. Indirect pathways dominated the influence of negative academic emotions. Conclusion This study identifies a pattern of associations consistent with the hypothesized emotion-cognition-behavior-outcome pathway in GenAI-supported learning. The findings offer empirical evidence for developing targeted academic-emotion-informed intervention strategies, improving students’ AI acceptance and learning engagement, and promoting the high-quality development of intelligent education.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping language learning in higher education, yet students’ engagement in AI-assisted language learning depends on more than access to technological tools. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) as an overarching theoretical perspective, this study examined how emotional intelligence and metacognition were associated with engagement directly and indirectly through enjoyment and self-efficacy, while also evaluating their predictive value. Survey data from 847 university students in China were analyzed using structural equation modeling and random forest analysis with repeated nested cross-validation. The SEM results showed that emotional intelligence and metacognition were positively associated with engagement, enjoyment, and self-efficacy, while enjoyment and self-efficacy were also positively related to engagement. All four indirect effects were significant. The extended random forest model achieved an out-of-sample R² of .472, improving R² by .081 over the baseline random forest and by .069 over the extended linear model. Emotional intelligence showed the highest permutation importance and revealed potentially nonlinear predictive patterns across individual learners. These findings highlight the complementary value of explanatory and predictive approaches for understanding engagement in AI-assisted language learning.

Agentic artificial intelligence extends delegation across networks of human and artificial agents. Research already examines delegated authority, autonomy, trust, accountability and coordination. This article addresses a complementary methodological question: how can agentic delegation, considered as a whole, be governed as a project? Drawing on established project management methodologies, including the Project Management Body of Knowledge, PRINCE2 and ISO 21502, the paper examines the transposition of project initiation, stakeholder identification, scope definition, planning, resource management, risk assessment, monitoring, change control, acceptance and closure. Particular attention is given to delegated autonomy, successive sub-delegations, alignment, semantic continuity and the preservation of governing constraints. The Agentic Delegation Charter is proposed as an adaptation of the conventional project charter, established at initiation as the constitutive reference for the delegation project. The paper advances a conceptual and methodological framework rather than an empirically validated governance model. Its limitations and directions for future evaluation are explicitly identified.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), synthetic media, social bots, and agentic AI are turning information disorder from a content-verification problem into a governance problem for multimedia information ecosystems. Research on fake news, deepfakes, GenAI misuse, and cyber-enabled influence has developed in largely separate streams, and none of these streams offers an integrated governance model for influence activity coordinated through AI-supported workflows. This study develops such a model through a structured evidence synthesis of 35 peer-reviewed sources published between 2019 and 2026, identified through four structured discovery queries and citation chaining and appraised with evidence-type-specific criteria. The synthesis identifies five mechanisms through which AI reshapes information disorder: influence orchestration, ambiguity production, selective persuasion, hybrid human–machine dissemination, and a trust paradox in countermeasures. On this basis, the study defines agentic influence operations as workflow-level risks and organizes them in a twelve-dimension framework that links AI capabilities, content modality, platform infrastructure, data access, evidentiary trust, organizational harm, and governance control points. It also sets out construct boundary conditions, five propositions with explicit evidence status, a managerial control set, and a phased implementation roadmap. Only the proposition on synthetic media and uncertainty about authentic evidence has direct empirical support; the others are offered for testing through simulation, experimental, design-science, and expert-validation studies.
